what: Delta parallel robot (Clavel type) – currently blocked. Three motors on the base, 120° apart, each drive a 48 mm upper arm through an 8:24 gear (3:1). From each arm a pair of parallel 56 mm lower links with ball joints runs down to a common tool head. The supplied program would solve the inverse kinematics for 13 XYZ waypoints, three pick-style stations, and run the three motors together. The model cannot be opened yet: it uses part 5996 six times, which Brickwright does not support, so neither the model nor its program can run.
try: The model is blocked: Brickwright refuses to load it until part 5996 is supported, so there is nothing to run yet. You can still read its program in Code to see how a Delta robot is controlled.

In the program, find the Vector leg script. For each arm direction φ (90°, 330° and 210°) it projects the target onto that arm’s vertical plane and solves one intersection: where can the elbow be so that it is 48 mm from the shoulder and 56 mm from the tool joint?

Compare the waypoints: the tool head first lifts 25 LDU (10 mm), then visits three stations 24 LDU (9.6 mm) from the centre and 120° apart, dipping 15 LDU (6 mm) at each. Predict which motors must move when the head only goes straight up.
Look at the guards: targets outside |x|, |z| ≤ 30 LDU or outside a 29 LDU height band, or shoulder angles outside 15°–40°, stop the program before any motor moves.
why: Each pair of lower links forms a parallelogram, so the tool head cannot tilt; it can only translate in x, y and z. Three motors give exactly these three degrees of freedom. Each leg is solved on its own: the shoulder sits 200 LDU (80 mm) from the centre and the tool joints 60 LDU (24 mm), so the effective offset is 140 LDU. The elbow must lie on a circle of radius L = 48 mm around the shoulder and on a sphere of radius l = 56 mm around the tool joint. That gives D·cos θ + y·sin θ = (L² + q² − l²)/(2L), solved as θ = atan2(y, D) − acos K. The motor target is −3·(θ − 35°), because the gear multiplies by 3 and the saved pose has θ = 35°.
matters: Delta robots are the fast pick-and-place machines of packaging lines and the frame of many 3D printers: the heavy motors stay on the base and only light rods move. The price is a nonlinear, coupled relation between motor angles and tool position, and a workspace limited by the arm lengths. The program shows the standard answer: compute the inverse kinematics for every waypoint and scale the three motor speeds so they arrive together. This experimental model has not been opened or measured in Brickwright; its mechanical behaviour is unverified.
question: The tool head rises straight up by 10 mm at the centre (waypoint 1). Do all three motors turn by the same angle? And when the head then moves 9.6 mm sideways to station 1?
answer: Straight up at the centre: yes. By symmetry each shoulder angle changes from 35° to about 19.5°, so in the program’s own equations all three motors turn by about +46.5°. Sideways to station 1: no. From the lifted pose the motor targets change by roughly −3.5° (A), −11.4° (B) and +3.0° (C). Even a straight sideways move needs three different motor motions, which is why the program scales the speeds so all three finish together.
further: Work through the leg equations by hand for waypoint 3 (x = −24, y = 192.47 LDU, z = 0) and check the three shoulder angles against the 15°–40° guard.
Compare Atlas Six (Stewart platform, six legs, six degrees of freedom) and Twinpoint (planar five-bar, two degrees of freedom): in all of them several chains share one end effector.
Before this model can teach anything in the simulator, part 5996 needs catalogue and geometry support. After that, construction, motion and tool-position accuracy all still have to be checked.
formula: Leg at angle φ: radial = x·cos φ + z·sin φ; D = 140 − radial; q² = x² + y² + z² + 140² − 280·radial; ρ = √(D² + y²); K = (L² + q² − l²)/(2Lρ) with L = 120 LDU (48 mm), l = 140 LDU (56 mm); θ = atan2(y, D) − acos K. Motor target = −3·(θ − 35°). Shoulders at φ = 90°, 330°, 210°. Coordinates in LDU, y downward.
